Hmm, trying to recall exactly what I was doing. I think I was contending with problems regarding how the core ResourceFormatLoaders would make assumptions about handling resources, even custom ones, that were resulting in exceptions being thrown. And I needed to get them to treat my resource (extending an in-engine type) the way they would have evaluated any other in-engine type with the same base class. So I simply said, "if you're a ResourceFormatLoader with a script, then treat it however you want. But if you don't have a script, then just think of it like you would its base class." Furthermore, if you are *extending* a class that expects a given extension, then I would expect that class to have some level of compatibility with the base extensions (again, like `.res` with all `Resource` types). body:
I initially tried to do it with the global class name stuff, but that alone didn't work. If you change a C# file and in so doing modify its global class name, then the C# file becomes a stale representation of the class information until the code is recompiled. But the engine doesn't dictate *when* the C# class gets recompiled, it's supposed to be driven by the user (e.g. running the compiler or playing a scene which auto compiles beforehand). And that's a separate process than the editorfilesystem gathering up global class names (which it might do quite regularly).

Furthermore, if you open up the editor after closing it, class names have to be loaded in from serialized metadata. They can't pull this metadata from the C# file because the script knows its name only when a compiled build of the script in an assembly exists (and there is none on first bootup), so there's literally no name for the C# file (or possibly a cached old one, iirc). Regardless, I remember that, to solve this issue, I had to create an entirely separate, secondary name caching-mechanism specifically for compiled languages to avoid issues with staleness of data.

body: That's not what the GDScript style guide says (although I'm not opposed to this change). It says that floats should have `x.0` or `0.x` instead of just `x.` or `.x`. In this case, `TAU` is a float, and in the expression `TAU / 4`, `4` is not technically a float, it's an integer which is implicitly converted to a float. According to the style guide, either `TAU / 4` or `TAU / 4.0` is appropriate. That said, `TAU / 4.0` is more explicit and likely better.

body:
Well, there are several problems with this approach, caused by the fact that I need to be able to access sub-properties of resources, while still being able to determine the owning object, as this is needed by the `add_undo_property(...)` function.

With a StringName, I cannot not access a sub-resource's properties (for example I could not use `get("texture.size")` in a Sprite2D node). So instead I though about using NodePath, which allow accessing sub-resources properties with a single string, but I have no way in such case to retrieve the Object owning the property, which is still needed by the `add_undo_property(...)` function.

If we go the NodePath route, I would likely need to add a new function, to retrieve the object owning a property. Right now we only have get_indexed(...) in Object that return the value, but no way to get the owning object. Using my previous example, `my_sprite_2D.get_indexed(..."texture.size"...)` returns the size value, and a new function `my_sprite_2D.get_indexed_object(..."texture.size"...)` would return the texture resource. I might also need a function to extract the property path for the whole path, like `my_sprite_2D.get_indexed_object(..."texture.size"...)` would return `"size"`.

That way I could solve the problem, but that's kind of more changes than what I propose here.

author: Duroxxigar

body: I don't have a strong opinion. Properties are more idiomatic for the Godot API in general, but that's not a strong rule. The most important is to have both an easy upgrade path from the earlier API, and a new API that is as consistent as possible with the future one in 4.0. If this was moved somewhere else in 4.0, then it doesn't matter too much how it's done in 3.x as it won't impact 4.0+ APIs.

Why not use forward slashes for the paths? Most Windows tools support them, and in this situation we are working entirely (?) within Python (these values end up in a `ToolsLocation` constructor after several `os.path.join` calls), so I assume forward slashes are preferred.

If not, then why prefer the `r"\"` syntax above, and `\\` here? The former seems more elegant, although I will note that VS Code's syntax highlighting does not highlight it correctly.

body:
Thanks for your work! I haven't tested yet, but I've left some comments about coding style.

Concerning your specific questions:

> What to do with the assertions? I think they may be too heavy to replace them with error macros, since that causes them to be left in for release builds, but I can't find how assertions are done in Godot.

What you can do is to wrap error calls with defines to avoid doing them in release, so they will show up only in the editor (it's configured in release_debug) and in game debug/release_debug.

Something like that:
```
#ifdef DEBUG_ENABLED
#define CHULL_ASSERT(m_cond) if (unlikely(!m_cond)) ERR_PRINT("Assertion \"" _STR(m_cond) "\" failed.")
#else
#define CHULL_ASSERT(m_cond)
#endif
```

> Is LocalVector the proper type to use here?

Yes, it's the proper type to avoid copy-on-write.

> Perhaps the custom classes PoolArray and Pool should be replaced with Godot's types (perhaps PagedAllocator) or even no pooling at all.

Yes, it looks like it would work well in this case! It should be fine to backport `paged_allocator.h` along with `spin_lock.h` (which you don't need in your case, but better keep things synchronized with master).

Since files are organized in a slightly different way on 3.x, `paged_allocator.h` should probably go to the core folder directly.

The trim actually wasn't present when I initially implemented this functionality, it was added in dc7f5557839b27831d284d44525a4b4815f4a46e (not sure why, but it looks ok).

Maybe you are getting this issue because the size of the match highlighting is determined *not* from the actual text being searched, but some label instead:
```
	match_rect.size.x = font->get_string_size(_search_text_label->get_text()).x;
```
And that label is set *before* `FindInFiles::start()` is called, see `FindInFilesPanel::start_search()`. Which means it won't have the trimming you added in the `FindInFiles` class.
Using a label meant for display here is a design mistake and should use the real pattern instead, or use the actual width of the search result text (this was also introduced by dc7f5557839b27831d284d44525a4b4815f4a46e)

Might be more reliable to use sed, grep or perl instead of relying on a specific order of words.
```
$ clang-format --version | sed "s/[^0-9\.]*\([0-9\.]*\).*/\1/"
12.0.0
```
This extracts the first occurrence of an uninterrupted string of numbers and dots (could be `..42.` too but a proper `12.0.0` number is more likely, unless some distros start injecting numbers before the clang version).

So,it would be better if we create a function I suggested before,

Or,in update methods, remove elements from slot_info Map, if they are greater than number of actual possible slots.
I don't think this second approach is any better.because it needs to wait for update notification.This also allows creating slots with no error but are removed immediately.

body:
I have a feeling that it is working by chance and that different settings won't produce the same nice results. We should come up with a more principled factor to reduce the amount of blur. 

_Edit: Let me think about this more clearly later, but it may be the case that the multipliers should just be 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125. What we need to figure out is the effective shadowmap resolution of each split. IIRC each split has half the resolution of the previous split, so the blur factor should be cut in half each time. Coincidentally, this results in splits very similar to your default of (1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1) above. I need to double check that that is how the splits work_
author: clayjohn

body:
The assumption of each split having half the resolution of the previous split is false, for a few reasons:
1) Each split has same Shadow map Resolution assigned to them (1/Split count of the total Atlas)
2) if Split 1 is 10% of the distance, and Split 2 is 30% of the max distance, the 2nd split isn't half the effective resolution of Split 1, as it's rendering 30%, including the 10% of Split 1, making it 1/3 of the effective resolution of Split 1.

Do keep in mind, the 10%,20%,50% splits are only the defaults.

Now that I think of it, there is possibly an easy way to Determine split blur probably...
When looking at the Default of 1 , 0.5 , 0.2 , 0.1 I notice a pattern. Default splits are 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.5 , 1
See where I'm going?
They're just in reverse order, which makes sense, as the effective shadow resolution is proportional to their size, and blur is connected to effective resolution so...
author: mrjustaguy

body:
I should try playing around with split values in DirectionalLight3D and see the automatically chosen blur values for each split still look good. I remember it working out just fine in practice, but I need to test it again just to make sure (and provide a MRP).

> What we need to figure out is the effective shadowmap resolution of each split.

As mrjustaguy pointed out, each split takes the same space within the shadow map, both when using PSSM 2 Splits and PSSM 4 Splits. It's just that more distant splits cover a larger area, and therefore have a lower texel *density*.
author: Calinou

body:
Right, so we are back to calculating the effective area based on split size. I guess we have two options then. We can adjust the blur amount with reference to the entire atlas, or with reference to the first split. 

I think adjusting with reference to the first split makes more sense (which is what this PR already does).

So, what we need to do is calculate the relative sizes one way of doing that is:
``shadow_split_offset.x / shadow_split_offset[i]``
With default values you get the same results as what you have (first split can still be hardcoded to 1.0). But with this, when you move away from default values the blur scale is determined with reference to the relative split size between the first split and the current split. Instead of being determined with reference to 1.0 and a different split.
*Before*
| split | size | blur_factor |
|-------|------|-------------|
| 1     | 0.1  | 1.0         |
| 2     | 0.2  | 0.5         |
| 3     | 0.5  | 0.2         |
| 4     |      | 0.1         |

| split | size | blur_factor |
|-------|------|-------------|
| 1     | 0.19  | 1.0         |
| 2     | 0.2  | 0.5         |
| 3     | 0.5  | 0.2         |
| 4     |      | 0.19         |

*After*
| split | size | blur_factor |
|-------|------|-------------|
| 1     | 0.1  | 1.0         |
| 2     | 0.2  | 0.5         |
| 3     | 0.5  | 0.2         |
| 4     |      | 0.1         |

| split | size | blur_factor |
|-------|------|-------------|
| 1     | 0.19  | 1.0         |
| 2     | 0.2  | 0.95         |
| 3     | 0.5  | 0.2         |
| 4     |      | 0.1         |

body:
I don't have any references, but I can give you an example.
For this example, let's say the tolerance `DUPLICATE_VERT_EPSILON` is such that two numbers that are an integer are apart are unequal. (e.g. 1 and 2 are different; 1 and 1.9 are equal). E.g. `#define DUPLICATE_VERT_EPSILON 0.99`

Now insert the vectors (0, 0, 0), (-0.9, 1, 0), and (-1.1, 1, 0); in this order. This yields the following tree:
```
             (0, 0, 0)
             /       \
 (-1.1, 1, 0)        (-0.9, 1, 0)
 /          \        /          \
```
(-0.9, 1, 0) is inserted right of (0, 0, 0), because the x compares equal, therefore the y coordinate determines that it is greater.
(-1.1, 1, 0) is inserted left of (0, 0, 0), because -1.1 does not compare equal to 0, and then compares as less, even with the tolerance.

However, (-1.1, 1, 0) and (-0.9, 1, 0) would compare equal; they are only 0.2 apart! But they never get compared with each other.


Yes, the VHACD approach looks interesting.

I would move this to after line 72, in the logic which handles the spinner being clicked.

When the mouse_pos is set here on line 105, when I let go of my mouse button the mouse does not appear _exactly_ where I pressed down, it can be quite a bit off depending on how I move my mouse.

body:
`p_markers` can't be created by `_print_var()` because the function is recursive. It is created by the actual `print()` function which is the only caller of the recursive `_print_var()`.

`p_markers` is only useful during `print()`, so it does not make sense to make it a member of `JSON`. Making it a member variable would also introduce potential race condition if `JSON::print()` is called by multithreaded code.

`Variant::stringify()` requires passing a similar structure to track circular structure:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/364ea7f280a3f074795e542b16b1d0ec76cf6ce2/core/variant/variant.cpp#L1626

body:
Indeed, I took things out of balance by adding the RAII (`MutexLock`) style and forgetting to remove some of the explicit unlocks.

By the way, this PR makes the same mistake. 😃 Please remove the explicit unlocks inside the `if`s where you have switched to the scoped lock style, and please do so also in `get_resolve_item_status()`, where I forgot myself.

Furthermore, I don't think it will actually impact performance, but it's even better to enclose each `MutexLock` declaration along with the code it protects in a scope so the lock is released earlier instead of at the end of the function. I don't know if the original intent of the code regarding the early-unlock was optimization or just to avoid writing the unlock call many times, but, in any case, it won't harm.

**UPDATE:** To elaborate, I didn't have a strong reason to keep the explicit lock/unlock or fully switch to the scoped style. I just decided on a per case basis judging which would be more readable, but now I think it's better to use `MutexLock` everywhere, at least in this class, for consistency.

`is_class()` uses strings and using strings is bad™. It's slower (not noticeably, but technically slower) and prone to mistakes. Not only you can misspell class name, when you rename class you might forget to rename all references and don't notice it until someone encounters some obscure bug. That said, you could change the ifs below to also use casting.

body:
What do you mean? 

count is either 4 or 8.

v.bones.size() is a number from 0 to +infinity.

uint32_t idx = 0; idx < vertex_array.size(); idx++

first iteration is:

1. idx = 0
2. Let's assume the bone size is 7
3. 
```
for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
    w[idx * count + j] = v.bones[j];
}
```
4. `idx = idx + 1` from `uint32_t idx = 0; idx < vertex_array.size(); idx++`

The second iteration is:

5. idx is 1
6. Let's assume the bone size is 6
7. 
```
for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
   w[idx * count + j] = v.bones[j];
}
```
8. `idx = idx + 1 ` from `uint32_t idx = 0; idx < vertex_array.size(); idx++`


`array.resize(varr_len * count);` Will always make the array a multiple of 4 or 8 so they probably should be zero initialized though..

body:
I agree. I'm pretty sure the original PR from @me2beats specifically called them `EditorAction` which was way more clear and in line with the expected concept. Ideally, a Command Pallete is merely *one way* in which a supposed `EditorAction` could be executed. Shortcuts are *another* way. But then you could also have entirely alternate, scripted means of executing an `EditorAction` (e.g. a custom EditorPlugin that applies a vim-like editing interface over the entire Godot Editor).

The `EditorAction`s shouldn't be tied directly to the notion of input events *or* shortcuts. They are simply a singular collection of globally accessible commands that can be categorized, filtered, sorted, executed, and contributed to by both engine code and script code.

Instead of using `erase`, you can append `"/"` *only* when it's not present yet.

You should also amend the commit to fix the code style (tabs for indentation, spaces around operators, trailing whitespace). Best practice when contributing to projects is to try to match the code style of nearby code. But we also use `clang-format` to enforce style, see https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/community/contributing/code_style_guidelines.html

Finally, this can crash if `name` is empty. This may or may not happen depending on the code that fills `recentd`, but it's still good practice to guard against a potential out of bounds read. The manual way would be `name.length() > 1 && name[name.length() - 1] == "/"`, but `String` also has more high level features that can simplify this code significantly: `name.right(1) == "/"` or even better `name.ends_with("/")`).

body:
Ah consequences of writing a PR at 3am .. you are absolutely right, the `alloc_count` returned by `scenario_owner.get_rid_count()` is the number of valid allocations, so we could either do this, or presumably have a function to return `max_alloc`.

I'm actually suspecting that the latter approach is better in some ways, as it makes it easier to iterate through the list and repeat a call `get_ptr_by_index` relatively cheaply. If you wanted to call only the _valid_ ptrs by index, it would presumably be very slow or require a secondary structure to do this.

Quite often I've noticed people using the pattern `get_ptr_by_index(10)` then a line later `get_ptr_by_index(10)`, so it would be nice to keep this cheap (ish).

The only downside is that in the thread safe version, even reading the invalid member contains a spinlock, so in a pathological situation could slow it down. What about having a separate function to return the next valid member of the list? Or we could use a more multi-function external iterator similarish to STL, however this might be overkill.

Looking at `get_owned_list` I remember you mentioning this last night, and it does exactly the same pattern with max_alloc, but getting the whole list each time is not ideal so I think one of these earlier two approaches are most preferable so far...
i.e.
* `next_index = get_next_valid_index(int p_index)`
* or a custom iterator

`RID_Alloc::allocate_rid()` and `RID_Alloc::initialize_rid()` are two APIs, so this situation will happen if only the former is called.

In this case, the `initialize_rid()` inside `RendererStorageRD::texture_2d_initialize()` will be skipped if `ERR_FAIL_COND` is triggered. No error handling can be done in `texture_2d_create()` (the `FUNCRIDTEX1` macro).

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/7a85e95a4b699960c540bb583cec526ab1b034d8/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/renderer_storage_rd.cpp#L543-L551

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/7a85e95a4b699960c540bb583cec526ab1b034d8/servers/rendering/rendering_server_default.h#L156-L165

The parameter range validations in this PR are added to prevent this error condition from happening.

You can avoid this by using a list and a string join:
```python
argtext = []
for i in range(argcount):
    argtext.append("m_type"+str(i+1))
argtext = ", ".join(argtext)
```

On top of that, the common for loop can also be removed, and with a bit of list-comprehension and fstring:
```python
argtext = ", ".join(f"m_type{i+1}" for i in range (argcount))
callargtext = ", ".join(f"const m_type{i+1}& arg{i+1}" for i in range(argcount))
callsiargs = ", ".join(f"Variant(arg{i+1})" for i in range(argcount))
[...]

I really think you should tune the quality parameter, preferably based on p_lossy_quality.  In fact, for BC7, it's probably better to leave flags at Default and tune the quality parameter instead.  Leaving it as 0 should probably only be done if you need maximum speed.  The quality increase at the low end of the quality scale is significant, and low values should still be much faster than the previous CVTT build.

Also, if you are going to do BC6H in the future then I'd recommend using Faster/Fastest flags sparingly there because BC6H_FastIndexing is prone to sparkly artifacts and most projects will have very few BC6H textures.

body:
@reduz The problem is that there is code where I don't know what subpass we're running especially once we make different breaks so we can support reads in the transparent pass. 

For instance if we don't need reads we can optimise by doing it as we do now:
- Pass 1 subpass 1 = Opaque
- Pass 1 subpass 2 = Sky
- Pass 1 subpass 3 = Transparent
- Pass 1 subpass 4 = Tonemap and copy to 2D buffer

Then if we have effects enabled that require reads we change it to:
- Pass 1 subpass 1 = Opaque
- Pass 1 subpass 2 = Sky
- Pass 2 subpass 1 = Transparent
- Pass 2 subpass 2 = Tonemap and copy to 2D buffer

And in the least optimal case, if we have glow or DOF turned on, or if we're rendering at half resolution, we end up with:
- Pass 1 subpass 1 = Opaque
- Pass 1 subpass 2 = Sky
- Pass 2 subpass 1 = Transparent
- Pass 3 subpass 1 = Tonemap and copy to 2D buffer

So we can see that for our transparent and tonemap/copy pass we can't hardcode the subpass, it changes depending on configuration.

body:
After discussion with maintainers, I agree with the change.

Conceptually, this is fine, a 2D/3D split marginally helps make the code organization better, but also paves the way to more possibility to decrease build size in custom 2D/3D only builds.

My main concern is with breaking compatibility on the include paths for C++ modules which use those Godot resources.
- For modules which only track a single Godot version (like in-house C++ modules for game-specific logic, etc.), it's fine, the devs can just do the same refactoring when updating to Godot 4.3.
- For general-purpose open source modules which aim to support multiple Godot branches, it's a bit trickier. They can still wrap things with `#if VERSION_HEX >= 0x040300` checks, though that implies including `core/version.h` in all affected files. Thankfully with GDExtension/godot-cpp, such modules are less common than they were in 3.x, so I think the tradeoff is acceptable (compatibility is not broken for godot-cpp as their the include paths are all flattened to a single folder).

body: I've tested all of the logic to these descriptions that I've added, and I can confirm that this method will return `true` if the Window is visible, but `false` if it's not (i.e "is it being drawn to the screen right now?"). Upon further testing this seems to also check if the Window is minimized or not when determining `can_draw`: https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62965063/124701056-e492ab00-debb-11eb-83d3-8f43d2f9fa54.mp4 However, this functionality is different than `Window.visible`, which doesn't check if the Window is minimized: https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62965063/124701489-b1045080-debc-11eb-945a-b6fe8604f3d1.mp4 That's the only thing I've found to be different. This difference exists because `Window.visible` only checks if the window is set to visible by the engine/editor, whereas `can_draw` actually checks whether the window is being _drawn_ to the screen _currently_. When the window is minimized it's obviously not being drawn to the screen, nor are any of the window's elements being redrawn, but when it's open it _is_ being drawn to the screen, and thus so are all of its child nodes. So my description is still accurate to what the method does.

body: What's the point to do `p_node->replace_by(rigid_body)` to then free `p_node`, and then assign it `rigid_body`? That's pretty confusing.
author: akien-mga

body:
In the case of p_node, this will be the root of the object which will by default be a Node3D type. For rigid bodies, we first want to use the replace_by function which will replace the Node3D node with a new RigidBody node. The root of this object now be a rigid body, and according to replace_by, the original node still exists, it's simply been removed from the tree.

The reason we call queue_delete on p_node now is since we have removed the original root node, I believe leaving it will cause a memory leak. This was simply to make it consistent with the behaviour of the other two switch cases which do similar things. We then assign p_node the new rigid body node, which has become the new root. This is because lower in the function, p_node is still consider as part of the function.

One thing I could do though is move the rigid_body->set_transform function above rigid_body->set_name which will make it more consistent with the other two switch cases, and hopefully a little less confusing.

```suggestion
            f"[Time elapsed: {int(elapsed_time_sec / 60)} minute{'' if 60 <= elapsed_time_sec < 120 else 's'} and {(elapsed_time_sec % 60):.1f} seconds.]"
```

`elapsed_time_sec  = 59` -> `0 minutes 59.0 seconds`
`elapsed_time_sec  = 60` -> `1 minute 1.0 seconds`
`elapsed_time_sec  = 120` -> `2 minutes 0.0 seconds`

`if elapsed_time_sec // 60 == 1` could be switched for `if 60 <= elapsed_time_sec < 120`
I tried both by using the below code in Python 3:

```
import timeit; timeit.timeit("elapsed_time_sec = 61; 60 <= elapsed_time_sec < 120", number=10000000); timeit.timeit("elapsed_time_sec = 61; elapsed_time_sec // 60 == 1", number=10000000)
```
with a range of different values instead of the 61. I found that the second option calculated small whole numbers a lot quicker, but the first one calculated both larger numbers and floats faster. For this reason, I chose to use the first option. If any better alternatives are available, please let me know!

body:
To support the [Android storage updates](https://developer.android.com/about/versions/11/privacy/storage) (which will include enforcing [scoped storage](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage#scoped-storage) with SDK 30, and will be required from 21 August 2021) will require a lot more work than this PR.

Scoped storage basically means that applications (that are not data management applications) will no longer be granted [`WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/Manifest.permission#WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE) permissions. To make this distinction clear, it has been replaced with the new [`MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/Manifest.permission#MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE) permission in SDK 30. With SDK 29 the revoking of `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permission could be delayed by setting the [`requestLegacyExternalStorage`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/R.attr#requestLegacyExternalStorage
) attribute which we did with Godot. However, with SDK 30, scoped storage will be enforced and Godot applications will no longer be granted `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permissions even with the `requestLegacyExternalStorage` attribute. Although, we can still set the new [`preserveLegacyExternalStorage`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/R.attr#preserveLegacyExternalStorage) permission to allow previously installed applications to continue to access data they previously had access to, which I suggest we do. Note: It will have no effect on new installs, which will be forced to use scoped storage.

With scoped storage Godot applications will be restricted to writing to the four application specific directories:
1. **[User files directory](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#getFilesDir()):** currently obtained using `get_user_data_dir()`. This location and data will always be available to the application. It counts towards the application data size, is inaccessible to other applications and will be encrypted on Android 10 and above.
2. **[User cache directory](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#getCacheDir()):** currently not obtainable, but should be implemented in Android now that #48544 has exposed `OS.get_cache_dir()`. This location is always available to the application, but Android may delete the data if available storage is low. As with the user data directory, it also counts towards the application data size, is inaccessible to other applications and will be encrypted on Android 10 and above.
3. **[User external files directory](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#getExternalFilesDir(java.lang.String)):** currently obtained using `OS.get_external_data_dir()`; therefore we should definitely not be reverting #49435. This location may not be available, but if it is, the data stored there will always be available to the application. Other applications with the required permissions can access this data.
4. **[User external cache directory](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#getExternalCacheDir()):** currently not obtainable, but should be added using, for example, `OS.get_external_cache_dir()`. This location may not be available, and if it is, Android may delete the data if available storage is low.

This has all been available since API level 8, and has not been affected by scoped storage. Note: external storage permissions were required to access the external storage locations before API 19, but setting `minimumSDK` to 19 will solve this. All these application specific data locations are associated with the application and will be deleted when the application is uninstalled.

The big challenge with scoped storage that needs to be addressed is making data available to other applications i.e. the problem raised with #45467 (changing it from just requiring documentation to a bug again) and I assume the driver behind #38913. Before SDK 29, media files could be shared with other applications by saving them to the media specific sub-directories under the directory returned from [`getExternalStoragePublicDirectory()`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/os/Environment#getExternalStoragePublicDirectory(java.lang.String)) and currently accessed using [`OS.get_system_dir()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_os.html#class-os-method-get-system-dir). This required the `WRITE_EXTERNAL_DATA` permission that is being revoked going forward. There was another problem that was never addressed (or even raised in #45467): once the data is saved there it requires the media to be scanned (using [`MediaScannerConnection.scanFile()`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/media/MediaScannerConnection#scanFile(java.lang.String,%20java.lang.String))) before it is available to other applications. Fortunately, this is done automatically by the device when it is rebooted, which provided a workaround, albeit a unsatisfactory one.

With scoped storage, the only way to save a file so it is available to other applications (and ensure it is not deleted when the application is uninstalled) we need to use the [`MediaStore` API](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/provider/MediaStore). With SDK 29, this is no longer restricted to just media files (Audio, Images and Video), but any type of file can now be saved to the [`MediaStore.Downloads`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/provider/MediaStore.Downloads) collection.

Fortunately, Godot currently only provides the ability to save one time of media file: Images. An image can be saved as a PNG file using [`Image.save_png()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_image.html#class-image-method-save-png). Unfortunately, the core code that enables this, currently uses the base `FileAccess` class to open the file that is written to:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9d4afa8b75f8db5ac039d6964c3e523119b750ca/drivers/png/resource_saver_png.cpp#L51-L70
So it can’t be simply overridden in the Android inherited version:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9d4afa8b75f8db5ac039d6964c3e523119b750ca/platform/android/file_access_android.cpp#L44-L61
Note: The Android inherited version currently doesn’t even support opening the file for writing:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9d4afa8b75f8db5ac039d6964c3e523119b750ca/platform/android/file_access_android.cpp#L51-L54

To support saving files that can be shared with other applications, we need to:
1. Create the Java files to write the file to the appropriate `MediaStore` depending on the MIME type.
2. Allow the Godot Android `FileAccess` class to call this method when saving a file that should be publicly accessible.
3. Create the Godot interface to be able to save files to the public locations (across platforms).
4. Update the `ResourceSaverPNG` code to not use the base `FileAccess` class so that platforms can override it.
5. Optionally, create similar code to enable saving of other media files both privately and publicly.

@godotengine/android @akien-mga I'm looking for feedback on this approach to easily provide support for shared and app specific storage.
For most platform, this argument doesn't make a difference (hence default to `true`). On Android (and maybe iOS), we send different paths depending on whether this is `true` or `false`.

The alternatives to this approach were either:
- Create an app specific dir enum that mirrored the `SystemDir` enum
- Or add app specific dir values to the `SystemDir` enum

body:
Note that this directly affects `TextEdit` input. Implementing the same behavior of the "Commit" button would lead to modification of in `_send_commit_msg()`. This will lead to workflow compatibility breakage in 3.x.

Currently, if no files are staged, then the informational hint below the button will display "No files added to stage" message when you press the "Commit" button, preventing the commit. In contrast, this PR at its state allows to commit immediately when typing out commit message, so that pressing <kbd>Ctrl + Enter</kbd> will stage all files automatically for you unless some files were already staged.

In other words, it may end up unexpected for existing users that pressing "Commit" button no longer prevents committing. Some users might still expect and want to stage all files (or some files) themselves manually rather than automatically before committing.

Note that I'm talking primarily in relation to 3.x, where I worked on this initially. The current approach is fairly risk-free, so regressions are unlikely to happen.

#ifdef FIRST_PASS

body:
Great work! Gravity override works well.

Apart from my review (mostly code cleaning) I have a couple extra comments:

- Please add a description for the PR - even if short - so there's a record in the future. You can indicate that it's based on the body implementation, link to fixed issue or addressed proposal when relevant (I think there was an issue about area gravity in this case). If you have a test project you can easily share (unless you use a MRP from a bug report) it can be a plus to help with reviewing, but it's not mandatory.

- This PR doesn't add support for Area scene nodes to detect soft bodies and notify scripts for custom code by users (like it's done for detected bodies and areas) so `monitored_soft_bodies` in `Area3DSW` is currently not used.

This will be needed eventually, but it can be added in a separate PR as it requires a few more steps to be functional:

-New method in PhysicsServer3D for soft body monitor callback: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fef27e9b5b9b125ff535513c80b45953e8717f7d/servers/physics_server_3d.h#L347-L348
(and implementation in PhysicsServer3DSW)

-Handle soft bodies in Area3DSW::call_queries(): https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fef27e9b5b9b125ff535513c80b45953e8717f7d/servers/physics_3d/area_3d_sw.cpp#L201
-Register monitoring callback in Area3D: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fef27e9b5b9b125ff535513c80b45953e8717f7d/scene/3d/area_3d.cpp#L280-L287

-Implement monitoring callback in Area3D, new method similar to bodies: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fef27e9b5b9b125ff535513c80b45953e8717f7d/scene/3d/area_3d.cpp#L139
 (it will need new specific signals for soft bodies)

 - New methods `get_overlapping_soft_bodies` and `overlaps_soft_body` exposed to script: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fef27e9b5b9b125ff535513c80b45953e8717f7d/scene/3d/area_3d.cpp#L560-L564
 
 -Updated documentation for new methods and signals in Area3D: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/doc/classes/Area3D.xml

after merging that PR, on line 400 of shader_forward_mobile.glsl you can add:

`layout(constant_id = 15) const float sc_luminance_multiplier = 2.0;`

This has two advantages. First is that you can also use it to divide at the end of the shader (and it will be turned to a multiplication by the compiler). Second, that in the clustered one you can simply do something like:

Once again, I did took care of manually testing it, but as [stated in the docs](https://curl.se/libcurl/c/curl_multi_wait.html):

> It will block until activity is detected on at least one of the handles or timeout_ms has passed.

Which means that when `timeout_ms == 0`, it **should not** not block indefinitely, since `0` milliseconds has already passed, no matter when you started.

Additionally, the docs states similarities with [`poll`](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/poll.2.html), so I would also think you can pass `-1` for a blocking behaviour (but I haven't tested that).

body:
We should try to copy how official .NET docs are written. They don't seem to use type references in place of nouns, neither in `summary` nor in `param` and `returns`.

See these examples:
- https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.vector3.lerp?view=net-5.0#System_Numerics_Vector3_Lerp_System_Numerics_Vector3_System_Numerics_Vector3_System_Single_
- https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.vector3.equals?view=net-5.0#System_Numerics_Vector3_Equals_System_Numerics_Vector3_

I think we should only add type references where it improves the documentation, and usually not when the signature already includes the type references.
When we do use a type reference, we should add something else to complete the noun. e.g.: `this <see cref="Color"/> structure` is better than `this <see cref="Color"/>`.

`.mobile` here doesn't mean the mobile renderer, but it's a feature override to know if we're running on desktop or mobile. So users can use the mobile renderer, but have different values configured for `force_blinn_over_ggx` depending on the platform.

So you shouldn't check the value with the `.mobile` suffix (I'm not even sure that works). The `.<feature>` part is checked by the engine as an override and will be applied to any use of `"rendering/shading/overrides/force_blinn_over_ggx"` (including the clustered one if running on mobile).

I actually removed the lock because it was a `SafeNumeric` and the queue is a fixed array so its size can't change.
I agree the status could no longer be `SafeNumeric`, but in any case the function probably does not need the mutex.

I would also amend the documentation, but before that I believe some more code changes need to be made that would affect the method descriptions. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I think you meant to expose some sort of virtual method that can be overridden? Virtual methods that can be overridden in the engine need to be marked with the `virtual` keyword. Virtual methods that we expose to the scripting API are bound to the ClassDB in a special way, and we usually prefix them with `_`. Check out how `_set_create_options` is implemented in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/editor/editor_resource_picker.cpp.

body:
I think acquire-release is probably fine everywhere except in SafeList but I find it very difficult to reason about these things so I'm not sure. I do think a system-wide barrier of some sort is appropriate during insertions or removals to SafeList because they tend to be fairly rare and the penalty if something goes wrong could be a double free or a use after free. These scalar values can absolutely have weaker guarantees.

The main thing we're attempting to avoid here is a sleeping on mutex contention, right? A memory barrier is not in the same league performance-wise as sleeping the audio thread.
author: ellenhp

body:
Apparently a compare-swap operation is [about as expensive as a cache miss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compare-and-swap#Costs_and_benefits) on x86 server platforms. I'm curious about other architectures but even if it were 100x more expensive than a cache miss I don't think I'd consider moving to another memory model for SafeList given how rarely insertions and deletions happen. I'm also hesitant to optimize without profiling results.

Side-note, thank you so much for reviewing this @RandomShaper. I know it's a difficult PR to review and I appreciate it. :)
author: ellenhp

body:
No worries! It's also hard for me to reason about every possible case. I just have the mindset of use acq-rel by default, which is already stronger than certain cases would need, but it still allows for more perfomant load/stores on some architectures than sequential would cause. When it's about compare-exchange, to be honest, I still haven't studied much about the performane consequences of using one memory ordering or the other.

In the case of `SafeList`, I can't but agree that the wisest thing is to leave sequential ordering.

This said, the only thing I'd ask you to do is switch to `SafeNumeric` in the other cases.

Doing the process in just one loop and removing the child bones for each bone is causing a regression when the bones are not sorted from root to leaves (if the root is last, all other bones are missing, since it removes its child bones).

Adding a first loop just for cleaning the child bones fixes the issue, but I wonder if there's a better solution (like sorting the bones beforehand).

You can reproduce the issue in @TokageItLab's project here: https://github.com/TokageItLab/3d-platform-test-for-godot4

body:
For what I've found `basename` and `get_basename` are not equivalent:

- `basename` returns the last component of the path, which could be a file name or a folder name. See http://man.openbsd.org/basename.3
- `get_basename` returns the path without the extension. See https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_string.html#class-string-method-get-basename

Given the name `file_name`, the fact that it will be used like this:

```
	String dest_path = trash_path + "/files/" + file_name;
```

*And as far as I can tell, `move_to_trash` does not work for folders.*

I think you should use `get_file` instead of `get_basename`. See https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_string.html#class-string-method-get-file

---

The behavior of `get_file` differs from the description of `basename` in that it will return empty string if the input is empty string or consist only of `/`. I quote from http://man.openbsd.org/basename.3:

```
If path consists entirely of ‘/’ characters, a pointer to the string "/" is returned. If path is a null pointer or the empty string, a pointer to the string "." is returned.
```

---

The description of `basename` at https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/basename.3.html (which that is not BSD) matches the description at http://man.openbsd.org/basename.3 and also provides some test cases:

```
              path       dirname   basename
              /usr/lib   /usr      lib
              /usr/      /         usr
              usr        .         usr
              /          /         /
              .          .         .
              ..         .         ..
```

Adding `get_basename` and `get_file` there for comparison, looks like this:

```
              path       dirname   basename   get_basename     get_file
              /usr/lib   /usr      lib        /usr/lib         lib
              /usr/      /         usr        /usr/            <empty string>
              usr        .         usr        usr              usr
              /          /         /          /                <empty string>
              .          .         .          <empty string>   .
              ..         .         ..         .                ..
```

Where `<empty string>` denotes the empty string.

You can see that if we assume we have a file path, then `get_file` is what we want.

body:
General implementation looks very good! I left a few comments for specific changes. 

I am concerned about how this interacts with our current scale_3d feature. I don't think we should expose a 3D scale and FSR together. I think the API should be like:
```
UpscaleMode:
* disabled
* bilinear
* FSR

If bilinear selected {
UpscaleAmount:
* 75%
* 50%
* 33%
* 25%
}
If FSR selected {
FSRQuality:
* Ultra Quality
* Quality
* Balanced
* Performance
* Custom
If Custom Quality {
fsr_custom_quality
}
fsr_mip_bias
fsr_upscale_sharpness
}
```

Does that make sense? Basically I don't think we should have the option of using scale 3D and FSR at the same time. Otherwise you will get users who use both together and wonder why their game looks horrible despite enabling FSR.

Also, it should be possible to make a version that works on the mobile renderer (using fragment shaders instead of compute), but that can be done in a follow-up PR if there is demand.

body:
```suggestion
			Sets scaling 3d mode. Bilinear scaling renders at different resolution to either undersample or supersample the viewport. FidelityFX Super Resolution 1.0, abbreviated to FSR, is an upscaling technology that produces high quality images at fast framerates by using a spatially aware upscaling algorithm. FSR is slightly more expensive than bilinear, but it produces significantly higher image quality. FSR should be used where possible.
```
author: clayjohn

body:
```suggestion
			Scales the 3D render buffer based on the viewport size uses an image filter specified in [member rendering/scaling_3d/mode] to scale the output image to the full viewport size. Values lower than [code]1.0[/code] can be used to speed up 3D rendering at the cost of quality (undersampling). Values greater than [code]1.0[/code] are only valid for bilinear mode and can be used to improve 3D rendering quality at a high performance cost (supersampling). See also [member rendering/anti_aliasing/quality/msaa] for multi-sample antialiasing, which is significantly cheaper but only smoothens the edges of polygons.
			When using FSR upscaling, AMD recommends exposing the following values as preset options to users "Ultra Quality: 0.77", "Quality: 0.67", "Balanced: 0.59", "Performance: 0.5" instead of exposing the entire scale.
```

body:
If there is only one flag, it is not possible to decide whether it is readonly by the inspector or property itself. For example, in the use case #30623, some properties will be readonly individually, but when the inspector becomes `readonly==true` due to other factors, and then the inspector itself becomes `readonly==false`, the readonly flag of all properties is set to `false`, so the properties can't be implemented readonly individually.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/51722#issuecomment-903155396
author: TokageItLab

author: TokageItLab

body:
> but when the inspector becomes readonly==true due to other factors, and then the inspector itself becomes readonly==false, the readonly flag of all properties is set to false, so the individual property's readonly becomes meaningless.

No, that's not how it should work. When changing the inspector's read_only status, you can simply re-create the whole tree to solve the problem by calling `update_tree()`. It's not the most efficient way but performance here is not a problem (changing the inspector read_only status is not something done very often). `update_tree()` should then set the property to read_only when either the property is set to read only or if the inspector is set to read_only.

Worst case you could have a `Map<EditorProperty*, bool>` to keep the individual properties' read_only status in the inspector, but it's not very worth it.

body:
For the area node, it would be more practical for the user to have just a `NodePath` property instead of entering the source and direction vectors by hand (the physics server parameters can stay the same though, since servers don't work with nodes).

You can set the property this way to restrict it to Node3D only:
`ADD_PROPERTY(PropertyInfo(Variant::NODE_PATH, "wind_source", PROPERTY_HINT_NODE_PATH_VALID_TYPES, "Node3D"), "set_wind_source", "get_wind_source");`
And then you can have just one member `wind_source_path` and set both source and direction from the `Node3D`.

What you can do then is to have a private method like `initialize_wind()` which sets the wind parameters in the physics server based on force, source and direction:
1. If force is < epsilon or source path is empty, just set wind force 0 and return
2. Get the `Node3D` node and set the source and direction based on its transform
```
Node3D *p_wind_source = Object::cast_to<Node3D>(get_node(p_wind_source_path));
ERR_FAIL_NULL(p_wind_source)
// Set force, source and direction in the physics server
```

The other thing to handle is that `get_node()` method can be called only when the node is already in the scene tree.

So in the wind source accessor, you can do this initialization only when the area node is in the scene (otherwise it would try to do it when the node is loaded but before it's added to the tree), checked this way:
`if (is_inside_tree()) { ... }`
That case in this accessor is for handling a change of wind source while the game is running.

And the second thing you would need is to do this initialization when entering the tree, in `Area3D::_notification` on `NOTIFICATION_ENTER_TREE`.

From the GLSL 120 spec:

> The relational operators greater than (>), less than (<), greater than or equal (>=), and less than or
equal (<=) operate only on scalar integer and scalar floating-point expressions. The result is scalar
Boolean. Either the operands’ types must match, or the conversions from Section 4.1.10 “Implicit
Conversions” will be applied to the integer operand, after which the types must match. To do
component-wise relational comparisons on vectors, use the built-in functions lessThan,
lessThanEqual, greaterThan, and greaterThanEqual.

That being said, you can still go back to the original mix implementation by constructing a ``vec3`` out of the ``bvec3``. E.g. instead of ``mix(a, b, lessThan())``, do ``mix(a, b, vec3(lessThan()))``

author: YuriSizov

body:
TBH, my plan is to move in the opposite direction.

We should have a general ERR_NOT_FOUND, not a special one that only some file methods return (because then this should be moved to a FileError enum).

Same for the permission one, that can be ERR_UNAUTHENTICATED. ERR_FILE_ALREADY_IN_USE can be ERR_ALREADY_IN_USE.

I also tried to keep these short and general, because while having whole sentences with explanations can be nice in some cases, it will read real weird or outright wrong in some cases the errors are currently used/returned.

So I deliberately did *not* move to prefixes and full sentences like in the link, because those context-dependent messages _should_ be provided by the application/game, not Godot, as Godot doesn't know the context. If we were to go that way, we'd need to split errors up into their own enums, and maybe create more expressive errors (like an Error class).

This PR is just trying to make sure the messages are general enough to make sense for the cases where Godot uses them.

I'm working on further PRs to:
- Remove current duplicate errors/merge some
- Add more errors for cases that currently aren't handled, and add them to methods (like file handling functions, and the networking ones could use more precise errors)

body:
It's a bit different from `stop_on_slope`. There's no notion of floor or walls, so yes it does affect all slopes. What `slide_on_slope` does is that when it's enabled the contact normals are equal to the slope normals, so the body is pushed back from the slope and slides along. When it's not enabled, ray shapes always use their own normal as contact normals, so the body is just pushed up and doesn't slide in slopes.

In practice, `slide_on_slope` doesn't affect `CharacterBody` much (except for the resulting normals) because this node has its own logic for sliding, but in the case of `RigidBody` with gravity applied it causes the body to slide down on slopes.

> By setting this, you cause it to be placed above the window. This means that none of the contents of the window this SurfaceView is in will be visible on top of its surface.

Which would mean that it would prevent additional component from rendering on top of the surface; is that the desired behavior?

author: m4gr3d

body:
> Which would mean that it would prevent additional component from rendering on top of the surface; is that the desired behavior?

Yes, this allows Godot rendering to be displayed on top, so a plugin can render behind the transparent surface, rather than always in front (like it does by default). As a side effect, plugins can't render on top of the surface when this is enabled, as you mentioned, but it's the only way I've found to achieve transparent rendering.

> Could you also walk me through how per-pixel transparency is achieved; it may help me understand better the logic in the PR.

Transparent rendering is achieved this way:
1. `per_pixel_transparency/allowed` & `per_pixel_transparency/enabled` are both set to true in Project Settings
2. `get_tree().get_root().transparent_bg = true;` is called at runtime to make the viewport transparent
3. At Android export time, `--translucent` is added to the command line (this step is needed on 3.x because `Main::setup()` is called after the surface is initialized, it won't be needed on master).
4. At Android runtime, `--translucent` command line is checked to create a surface with transparent capabilities (on master it will just check the project settings directly)
5. When the plugin is initialized, its own rendering frame is placed on top of the main frame by default, so this can be used to move it behind:
```
ViewGroup parentView = (ViewGroup)pluginFrame.getParent();
parentView.removeView(pluginFrame);
parentView.addView(pluginFrame, 0);
```
(from what I've seen, both this and `setZOrderOnTop(true)` are needed for transparency to work correctly)

The result is the plugin does its custom rendering (for example camera preview) and Godot draws on top of it with transparent background (for example to add UI elements).

Let me know if there's more I can clarify!

body:
No worries!

> Regarding ordering of the surface and of the plugins' views, we control that logic [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/e44379612d09a7b134bdadb901de409db170268c/platform/android/java/lib/src/org/godotengine/godot/Godot.java#L390) and [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/e44379612d09a7b134bdadb901de409db170268c/platform/android/java/lib/src/org/godotengine/godot/Godot.java#L400), so couldn't just have a flag that tells us if `translucent` is enabled, and changed the order of the views as shown in your sample code?
> With that approach, would we still need to set the `setZOrderOnTop(...)` flag?

I'm not sure why (it could be the way GL surfaces work), but both are needed for the system to work correctly.
I've tested again since last time and here's how it goes:
-`setZOrderOnTop` is needed for transparent rendering, without it the Godot surface renders with black background and any view behind it is not visible.
-Changing the order of views is not strictly needed if `setZOrderOnTop` is set, but it helps with inputs as it allows Godot inputs to be taken over views placed behind.

> Also, when you say the surface is transparent, does that mean that any view(s) `behind` it will be visible? I'm trying to clarify here since making the background transparent in Godot may not mean the same as making the surface view background transparent (which would allow to see underlying views).

Yes, it allows other views to be visible behind it.

Using this feature, you can also make a transparent app and see the device desktop in the background. But that requires to also change the style of the main Godot app to this:
```
<style name="GodotAppMainTheme" parent="@android:style/Theme.Black.NoTitleBar.Fullscreen">
     <item name="android:windowIsTranslucent">true</item>
     <item name="android:windowBackground">@android:color/transparent</item>
</style>
```

So far I haven't found a nice way to enable it in the export process or by code, but it would be a nice addition to this PR.

author: m4gr3d

body:
> Can you double-check that setZOrderMediaOverlay doesn't have a similar behavior to setZOrderOnTop (i.e: can it be used instead?).

No, I've just tested and with `setZOrderMediaOverlay` the Godot view still renders with black background and other views are hidden behind so it looks like `setZOrderOnTop` is needed.

> Okay, can we do that automatically then when the translucent flag is set (like I described above), this way the plugin itself won't need to move its own view.

Yeah it would be great to have a helper for that! Should it be optional though? Maybe something like a plugin function `is_view_behind()` or `get_view_order()`.

The reason is there are two possible states at the moment:
-Either you change the view order and you detect inputs in the godot view, but the plugin rendered behind doesn't get any input (can be useful for adding buttons on top of the plugin view)
-Or you don't change the view order and the plugin receives inputs, but not the godot view (can be useful if you want to render on top of a plugin but keep the plugin responsible for inputs)

body:
Great job! It's really nice to have more options for physics collision in the import process.

Apart from my review comments, I have one general concern about the VHACD options:
Is it really useful to expose all possible options for VHACD? Users might be lost with too many settings they don't understand and some settings don't seem to really make a difference in the results (or just cause them to be worse).
What do you think of exposing just a few settings that we know are going to make a difference and that we can document properly?
So far it seems to me that the only obvious ones would be the max number of convex hulls and the max number of vertices per convex hull.
But we can add more if you spotted some other ones that can be useful.

As a side note, I've tried to play with all the settings and I still have a hard time generating more than one simplified convex hull instead of actually decomposing for some models. I wonder if there's a general issue with VHACD or in the way we setup the faces.
If you have some examples of models for which you're able to get proper decomposition, I'm interested for testing purpose :)

And the last thing I would like to point out is a list of possible improvements to this process (but not necessary for this PR):
- As already mentioned, it would be nice to display the number of vertices in the generated convex hull while in this window. I would also add the number of convex hulls that result from the decomposition.
- Being able to reset the VHACD settings to default would be nice, it's easy to get lost with so many of them (but that might be unnecessary if we reduce the number of settings).
- It would be great for the primitives to get default sizes based on the mesh AABB so you don't have to do it by hand for obvious cases (or just little adjustments).
- There's a bug in the ui that prevents using the property sliders: left click and drag is detected by the preview window to rotate the model even when clicking in the settings. It might also require the preview to have a timer before generating the new convex hull so it doesn't freeze while changing the slider value.

body:
This paramter is quite important, together with `resolution` and `max_convex_hulls`. By setting it to `0.001` you are telling VHACD to consider really little concavity and so introduce another shape.

For example, if you set:
```
max_convex_hulls: 1024
max_concavity: 0.001
```
This will generate a lot of shapes, that will describe the Mesh silhouette really well.

If you set something like:
```
max_convex_hulls: 1
max_concavity: 0.001

// or
max_convex_hulls: 1024
max_concavity: 1
```
It will generate only 1 Collision shape that tries to describe the mesh silhouette as best as it can with just one convex shape.

This assumption is given by the fact that the artist/dev will need to explicitly add to the mesh name: `-convcol`, to trigger this code path, so it's reasonable that such shape is optimized to be a convex collision.

body:
It's not that easy to decide, because from what I understand there are actually two scenarios for `-convcol`/`convcolonly`:
1. Some users make a mesh without caring too much if it's convex or concave, and expect the import process to make it usable for physics.
2. Some other users make it convex on purpose, and expect the import process to keep it intact for accuracy purpose.

I would tend to support the case 1 by default, because that's the case users with less knowledge about physics will hit. Users in case 2 know what they are doing so they mostly just need some options to support this case.

So I would rather keep convex decomposition by default, and my plan is to add at least another variant like `-singleconvcol`/`-singleconvcolonly` to handle the other use case.

Does that make sense to you?

body:
`-` cannot be part of a valid identifier, so I don't think we need to document how `-` behaves with this method, just like how we don't document `+` or `*` or `/` behave.

Why `ToHtml5` -> `to_html_5` but `ToHTMLElement` -> `_to_html_element`? The latter should be `to_html_element`. In other words, the first character of a PascalCase identifier should not be prefixed with an underscore, and the only way to get an underscore prefix should be to start with one like `_ToHTML5` -> `_to_html_5`.
author: aaronfranke

body:
> Why `ToHtml5` -> `to_html_5` but `ToHTMLElement` -> `_to_html_element`? The latter should be `to_html_element`. In other words, the first character of a PascalCase identifier should not be prefixed with an underscore, and the only way to get an underscore prefix should be to start with one like `_ToHTML5` -> `_to_html_5`.

Because this is how it is implemented.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c5f62fad90f6b324e8d05ec4a8342e69b8af5507/core/string/ustring.cpp#L976-L1015

</details>

I just added the binding, documentation, and ported the code to C#.

Capitalized words, ACRONYMS and numbers are separated by adding `_` before the beginning of the character group. Other characters are not considered. Because of this, there is a duplicate underscore, and this is probably a bug.

Perhaps an example with `lowercase = false` will help you better understand how this function works.

```
ToHtml5 ToHTMLElement toHtml to_html TO_HTML A_B-C.D
To_Html_5 _To_HTML_Element to_Html to_html _TO__HTML _A__B-_C._D
to_html_5 _to_html_element to_html to_html _to__html _a__b-_c._d
```

If you think that this needs to be fixed, then this is a separate question. But I can try to fix it. Is this the option it should be:

```
ToHtml5 ToHTMLElement toHtml to_html TO_HTML A_B-C.D
To_Html_5 To_HTML_Element to_Html to_html TO_HTML A_B-C.D
to_html_5 to_html_element to_html to_html to_html a_b-c.d
```
?

> `-` cannot be part of a valid identifier, so I don't think we need to document how `-` behaves with this method, just like how we don't document `+` or `*` or `/` behave.

`-` used in filenames, commands, identifiers in some programming and markup languages.

body:
Ok, so here's the deal.

Sorry that you wrote all the code in MeshDataTool::set*custom but it's incomplete and complicated to get right, not to mention the need to switch formats.

So I want to suggest a different approach for the type conversion, which should have minimal performance overhead given that you are already doing the conversion in a loop.

In `create_from_surface`, on lines 167..175, I would like to suggest that we add conversion code, possibly done as a switch statement, to convert whatever internal format is in `cuf` or `cuu` into a Color. That way, all the user-facing functions can simply work with Color's and not have to do any conversion.

Also, as a user, I would want the API to be simple: just because I want to save half the space on my UVs shouldn't force me to write my own half->float conversion in gdscript or whatever. (Also, it seems that MeshDataTool isn't designed with performance in mind, so let's not worry about performance here)

If you would like help with it, I have some reference conversion code you can try copying here:
uint16_t* -> float*:
Import core/math/mathfuncs.h and use one of the `halfbits_to_floatbits` type functions.
(to get uint16_t* you can just cast the byte* to uint16_t*. The endianness is already guaranteed to be native)

uint* -> float* (UNORM, SNORM conversion) will look something like:
```cpp
bool is_signed = custom_type[i] == Mesh::ARRAY_FORMAT_RGBA8_SNORM 
float sign_mul = is_signed ? 2 : 0
float divisor = is_signed ? 127.0 : 255.0
...
	float result = ((cuu[j] - sign_mul * (found & 0x80)) / divisor)
```
I wasn't able to find an example of this conversion in godot code. You might be one of the first people to connect the dots of the internal vertex format and the user, so I guess you get to be the guinea pig for this code ;-)

Analogously, we will want the reverse code in `commit_to_surface`. To do the reverse, it is probably something like
```
	uint8_t result = (uint8_t)round(CLAMP(divisor * (floatval + sign_mul * (floatval < 0)) + 0.5, 0.0, 255.0));
```

I can't guarantee my unorm and snorm code is correct. we will need to test it. also watch out for NaN's. I think CLAMP should prevent NaN but still good to make sure.

author: reduz

body:
Scaling beyond 1.0 makes it possible to achieve supersampling in a way that's cheaper and easier than using a viewport with a larger size. While supersampling is not very practical for games, it's useful for [offline rendering](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3083), promotional/marketing screenshots, user-accessible photo modes, etc.
Supersampling is the best way to combat specular aliasing in Godot right now, at least until TAA is implemented (which is still a while away).

I've tested this and it works exactly as expected. Let's make high quality screenshots the norm 🙂 

However, there is no point in using a scale factor above 2.0 (due to how linear filtering without mipmaps works). I should probably clamp it to 2.0 if not done already.

author: reduz

body:
I still think there is a big problem with this approach, and is the fact that for generating sound from the main thread via AudioStreamGenerator, you need to access and keep the playback object. This will be also likely needed if something like VoIP is implemented, as you need to push the sound that comes from the network via a ringbuffer.

I think we could work around this by using the following logic:

* If the stream is polyphonic, we do things as-is, current code-path is used.
* If the stream is monophonic, we request and cache the AudioStreamPlayback and use a single sized stream_playback, and never free it until the stream is changed or removed.

Did some digging into this, I think the cause is setting the shortcut context [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/editor/plugins/script_text_editor.cpp#L1907) to the `ScriptEditorBase`. As the `FindReplaceBar` is not a child to the `ScriptEditorBase` the shortcut is not triggered. 

The `ShaderTextEditor` doesn't have this problem because the `FindReplaceBar` is a child of it. But, by handling it in `CodeTextEditor` we prevent the input propagating to it.

So this seems to be the correct approach to me, though it might be worth moving this to the `FindReplaceBar` itself so it's a little more self contained.

The idea with this part was to expose the necessary surface so that users could choose how they ask for visibility checks.

`is_visible_in_tree()` now automatically checks the viewport for what cull mask it is rendering.
`is_visible_in_tree_ignoring_cull_masks()` behaves as `is_visible_in_tree()` prior to the PR.
and `is_visible_in_tree_with_cull_mask(p_mask)` is exposed for clients in gdscript because as you say, it's impossible to account for how people will use it and what they expect.

I may have fudged the boundaries of what `is_visible_in_tree()` is for... I will admit. I didn't want to balloon the PR. Currently all of the UI/Control code expect visibility to coincide with rendering. It may be possible to sift through all of the UI code and replace each `is_visible_in_tree()` with a call that also checks the cull mask. author: akien-mga

body:
Usually 2d data is stored in a contigous block of memory in a row-after-row manner (that's the case for the `Image`) so when iterating over that data it's better to iterate over the rows in the outer loop to make the iteration happen sequentially over the memory (which is cache-friendly so most likely less memory reads will be needed). If iterating over the columns first you'd keep jumping back and forth over the memory.
Maybe compiler would optimize it anyway, maybe not, no idea. It's just better/safer to iterate row first in such cases.

Visualisation:
```
Image:
abc
def
ghi

In memory:
abcdefghi

Iteration order (row-first):
abcdefghi

Iteration order (column-first):
adgbehcfi
```
author: kleonc

body: I think it makes more sense logically anyway, since row first goes left to right, then top to bottom, which is how code is read, as opposed to column first, which goes top to bottom, then left to right.

body:
I appreciate the work done here and there's a lot of good stuff, but it's very hard to review.

Mixing code refactoring, code logic changes (impossible to spot in the huge refactoring), adding new methods, binding existing and new methods, improving documentation and tests all in the same commits means that basically this is all or nothing, and code review is impossible. This also makes it near impossible to discuss on the finer points where you decided to change the API (without following the proposals procedure).

I agree with most changes yet there are some I disagree with, and doing all this in-depth review of whether we want even more replace functions, or change the behavior of quoting methods, or break compatibility by changing the polarity of case (in)sensitivity checks... this is just to much for a single code refactoring PR.

So I would suggest splitting this PR into separate commits, and split some of the changes into separate PRs that will depend on this refactored one:

- Code readability refactoring (moving definitions around, renaming parameters, removing unnecessary `const` if you want but nothing more than that). Engine behavior and API should be unchanged.
- Documentation and test improvements for the existing API.

Then follow-up PRs can be made to evaluate the other changes you propose:

- Binding more existing methods and adding their documentation and tests.
- Changing case sensitivity logic (breaks compat)
- Changing quoting logic (breaks compat - btw likely also breaks engine features, but we'll discuss that in that PR)
- Adding more replace methods
- Maybe more that I missed in the huge diff

`rreplace` makes replacement starting from the right of the string. In a simple example:
```gdscript
"a a".replace("a", "B", 1) # prints "B a"
"a a".rreplace("a", "B", 1) # prints "a B"
```
In the above example, these calls are equivalents of `String.replace_first` and `String.replace_last` functionality-wise and I realized this after updating those functions. Will open a proposal noting this, and to discuss whether we want to coalesce these.

body:
This beautiful casting that you see right here (:p) tells the compiler which overloaded function to use.

The underlying cause is that in this PR I've overloaded all these functions with equivalent implementations that make use of C-strings (`const char *`) for performance reasons. On a more concrete example, just consider the following two function signatures:

```cpp
String String::find(const String &)
String String::find(const char *)
```

From a GDScript standpoint, nothing changes since the casting above chooses the right function signature which is the first one you see above, but from the C++ side, it makes the engine more efficient by avoiding `String` object allocations (which in turn avoid `CowData<T>` object allocations, plus `malloc` that in turn fire system calls to allocate the memory the `String` is going to use to the `char32_t` string itself). So from the C++ side, calls to `String::find("my_pattern")` are more effective, but the same function can also be called with `String` objects instead of `const char *`

Since you are adding all your libraries to the main "env" LIBS, not creating a separate environment would mean this shared library would have itself on the link line (shared libraries observe the LIBS var while static libraries do not). This manifest's specifically as a dependency cycle from scons.

Really your overuse of the main monolithic env is a bit trouble some. It's just conflates and entangles things. Cloning is very useful for branching your environments to be more specialized for any given build task or tasks.

If it was desired, I would redesign much of the godot build to not so heavily use the common main env, and instead do a lot more branched cloning.

Just left a couple nitpicks but it looks great and it's working fine (apart from the bug we already discussed and we're still investigating on the physics side).

**Edit:** Update about the character platform bug:
After investigation, it's due to changing the tilemap to use a separate body for each tile. CharacterBody2D applies the platform motion while ignoring the platform itself, but the way it works at the moment it can still collide with the next tile.
~It's most likely something that can be fixed in the physics system though, not a tilemap bug, so it's still all good :)~

**Edit 2:**
Actually this problem is a bit more complicated, because in order to handle platforms properly, we need all the tiles to either use the same body id, or get attached to the same object id and with this PR both of them is different for each tile.

@groud Would it be ok to change the design a bit in order to handle this case? Like attaching the Tilemap object itself to all tiles, and then have an API in the tilemap to retrieve the tile information (maybe from the body id).
I think that would also be better to be able to retrieve the TileMap itself from physics queries, which (unless I'm missing something) is not possible with the new design.
If needed we can discuss a bit more in details in the chat.

That's a bit too steep, we still support building Godot on fairly old distros which may not have SCons 4.2.0 packaged yet (as a matter of fact almost no distro has it packaged *right now* - only Arch Linux and Fedora).

There are Godot packages in Linux distro and they rely on system SCons, so they can't just pull it from the pip repos.

Instead, you should check the SCons version at runtime to conditionally support ninja build for SCons 4.2.0 or later, as we do for the compilation DB:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/3ca2a48767486a52bf4ec5b784a25a1beb2a3f50/SConstruct#L355-L362

(Might also be worth considering if this API or a similar one could be promoted to public in SCons upstream.)

body:
I'm not absolutely sure this would give the correct impression. In the vast majority of cases fast _isn't_ low quality, it is just faster. If an object is not rotating at all, fast produces the exact same result as high quality, and unless an object is rotating at high angular velocity, the quality of fast is not significantly worse than high quality.

If we call something "low quality", people are more likely to assume that they need to use "high quality" for the best result, whereas this is not the case here. "fast" is purposefully vague on this, and the tooltip points out that "high quality" is advantageous only in some specific situations.

Perhaps a compromise would be to make this distinction clearer in the tooltip?

EDIT: I've done the above. If there's a clear consensus to change this to "low quality" we can though. :slightly_smiling_face:

body:
I dont think all of the overloads you added are supported. 

Here is what the spec has to say:

> When the built-in functions are specified below, where the input arguments (and corresponding output) can be float, vec2, vec3, or vec4, genType is used as the argument. Where the input arguments (and corresponding output) can be int, ivec2, ivec3, or ivec4, genIType is used as the argument. Where the input arguments (and corresponding output) can be uint, uvec2, uvec3, or uvec4, genUType is used as the argument. Where the input arguments (or corresponding output) can be bool, bvec2, bvec3, or bvec4, genBType is used as the argument. For any specific use of a function, the actual types substituted for genType, genIType, genUType, or genBType have to have the same number of components for all arguments and for the return type. Similarly for mat, which can be any matrix basic type.
(pg 80 https://www.khronos.org/registry/OpenGL/specs/gl/GLSLangSpec.3.30.pdf)

``step()`` for example has two overloads:

> genType step (genType edge, genType x)
genType step (float edge, genType x)

So I don't think that the overloads added are valid.

body: Probably a dumb question but why is it `* scale` on `x` and `z`, and `/ scale` on `y`?
author: BastiaanOlij

body:
scale is basically just the "vertical radius", so you can think of a the ellipsoid as a unit sphere scaled by "scale" in the y axis and by "radius" in the x and z axis.

Because of this, the normal actually needs to be scaled in the x and z axis by `scale`, and in the y axis by `radius`. This is a particular case of using the transpose of the inverse of the transform matrix, which one usually does when transforming normals. See my explanation in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/51995.

The `/scale` factor on `y` comes from the fact that `y`is already scaled vertically  (since `y = scale * cos(Math_PI * v);`), so by dividing by scale we get `cos(Math_PI*v)`

To sum up:
If `(x,y,z)` is a point in the unit sphere, the (not normalized) normal of the scaled ellipsoid is given by:
`normal = (x*scale,y*radius,z*scale)`
